items.prompt: Trailhead's old nav sorted a rain jacket under 'Apparel' because that's its warehouse category. What kind of model does that reflect, and what's missing?
choices: The mental model — because shoppers think of clothes as Apparel too
The implementation model — how the system/business organizes things internally — with no translation into how shoppers actually think about their task
Neither — warehouse categories aren't a model at all
The mental model, but only for warehouse staff shopping on the site
items.explanation: Apparel/Hardgoods/Footwear reflects the business's internal stock structure — the implementation model. A shopper thinking 'I'm going hiking' is using a different, task-based mental model; IA fails when the implementation model is exposed directly as the nav instead of being translated.
items.reference:
Implementation model

How the business/system organizes things internally

Mental model

How the visitor naturally groups things in their head

Why: IA fails when the implementation model leaks straight into the nav instead of being translated into the visitor's model.

items.prompt: A visitor thinks 'I'm going hiking' before ever seeing a menu. Which model does that phrase describe?
choices: The mental model — how the visitor naturally frames their own goal, independent of how the system stores anything
The implementation model
A labeling system
A navigation system
items.explanation: The visitor's own framing of their goal, formed before they see any menu, is the mental model. It exists independently of whatever the backend or warehouse calls things — IA's job is to build a nav that matches this, not the system's internal structure.
items.reference:
Implementation model

How the business/system organizes things internally

Mental model

How the visitor naturally groups things in their head

Why: IA fails when the implementation model leaks straight into the nav instead of being translated into the visitor's model.

items.prompt: Why did the same rain jacket sit at only 34% findability under the old nav, despite being fully in stock and correctly listed?
choices: Because the mental model and the implementation model disagreed about where it belonged, and the nav reflected only the implementation model
Because the photo or price was wrong
Because search was disabled
Because too few people wanted a rain jacket
items.explanation: The product was accessible and accurately listed — the failure was purely structural: the taxonomy matched the warehouse's mental model, not the shopper's, so shoppers using their own (activity-based) model had no matching path.
items.reference:
Implementation model

How the business/system organizes things internally

Mental model

How the visitor naturally groups things in their head

Why: IA fails when the implementation model leaks straight into the nav instead of being translated into the visitor's model.

items.prompt: 'Hardgoods' accurately describes tents, stoves, and carabiners inside outdoor retail. Why can it still be a bad nav label?
choices: It's accurate but internal — a shopper outside the industry has never heard the term and can't map it to what they're looking for
It's too short
It doesn't fit on mobile screens
It's not accurate enough
items.explanation: A label can be technically correct and still fail — 'accurate but internal' labels work for people who already know the industry's vocabulary and fail everyone else, which for most nav is the majority of visitors.
items.reference:
🏭 Accurate but internal — 'Hardgoods'
🌫️ Ambiguous — 'Gear'
🎯 Task-aligned — 'Camping'

Why: a label has to pass one test — does it match what the visitor is trying to do, not how the business files it internally.

items.prompt: Which label is most likely to actually help a shopper trying to find gear for their first camping trip: 'Hardgoods,' 'Gear,' or 'Camping'?
choices: 'Hardgoods,' because it's the most precise internally
'Gear,' because it's short
'Camping,' because it matches the visitor's task rather than the store's internal category or an overly broad catch-all
All three work equally well
items.explanation: 'Hardgoods' is internal jargon and 'Gear' is too broad to narrow anything down. 'Camping' passes the actual test a label needs to pass: does it match what the visitor is trying to do.
items.reference:
🏭 Accurate but internal — 'Hardgoods'
🌫️ Ambiguous — 'Gear'
🎯 Task-aligned — 'Camping'

Why: a label has to pass one test — does it match what the visitor is trying to do, not how the business files it internally.

items.prompt: Trailhead's rain jacket is in stock, correctly priced, and fully functional to buy — yet it generated 40 support tickets in a month. What does that show about findability?
choices: A feature or product that can't be found is effectively unavailable to most people looking for it, regardless of whether it technically exists
Findability only matters for brand-new products
Support tickets are unrelated to IA
The product must have had a real defect
items.explanation: Findability failures don't show up as bugs — they show up as abandoned carts, support tickets, and 'we already built that' surprises. A product nobody can find might as well not exist for the visitors who never reach it.
items.reference:
34%found the rain jacket, old nav

Why: an unfindable feature is functionally unavailable — it shows up as tickets and abandoned carts, not bugs.

items.prompt: A team ships a genuinely useful feature but buries it three unexpected clicks deep. Users keep requesting the same feature the team already built. What's the most likely explanation?
choices: The users didn't read the release notes
The feature isn't actually as useful as the team thinks
Findability, not usefulness, is the bottleneck — a feature nobody can reliably locate gets used by almost nobody who'd want it
This only happens with free features, not paid ones
items.explanation: Repeated requests for something that already exists is a classic findability symptom, not a signal the feature lacks value. The fix is structural (where it lives in the IA), not a rewrite of the feature itself.
items.reference:
34%found the rain jacket, old nav

Why: an unfindable feature is functionally unavailable — it shows up as tickets and abandoned carts, not bugs.

items.prompt: In IA terms, what's the difference between a 'taxonomy' and a 'hierarchy'?
choices: They're the same thing with different names
A taxonomy is the set of categories and rules for what belongs where; a hierarchy is how those categories nest into a tree
A taxonomy only applies to search, a hierarchy only applies to navigation
A hierarchy is only used for websites with fewer than 10 pages
items.explanation: Taxonomy defines the categories and their membership rules ('what belongs in Hiking'); hierarchy defines how those categories nest relative to each other (Home > Hiking > Rain jackets). They're related but distinct: you can have the right categories nested in the wrong shape, or vice versa.
items.reference:
Home
↓
Hiking
↓
Rain jackets

Why: hierarchy is the nesting shape (the tree); taxonomy is the category rules that decide what goes where in it.

items.prompt: Trailhead's nav goes Home > Hiking > Rain jackets. What is this an example of?
choices: A labeling system only
A hierarchy — a tree showing what's nested under what
A card sort
A search system
items.explanation: This three-level path is the hierarchy in action: each category is nested under the one above it, forming a tree the visitor navigates level by level.
items.reference:
Home
↓
Hiking
↓
Rain jackets

Why: hierarchy is the nesting shape (the tree); taxonomy is the category rules that decide what goes where in it.

items.prompt: The top menu bar on Trailhead's site — visible on every single page — is an example of which navigation system?
choices: Local navigation
Contextual navigation
Global navigation — present everywhere, regardless of what page you're on
A taxonomy
items.explanation: Global navigation is the always-visible wayfinding, typically the top bar or main menu. It doesn't change based on which page you're currently viewing.
items.reference:
🧭 Global — every page
📍 Local — within one section
🔗 Contextual — inside specific content

Why: each system answers 'where am I and where can I go' at a different scope — mixing them up clutters pages with the wrong kind of link.

items.prompt: A 'you might also need trekking poles' link that only appears on the rain jacket's own product page is an example of which navigation system?
choices: Global navigation
Contextual navigation — tied to the specific content it appears on, not shown elsewhere
Local navigation
A card sort
items.explanation: Contextual navigation lives inside specific content and only makes sense there — unlike global nav, it isn't meant to appear on every page.
items.reference:
🧭 Global — every page
📍 Local — within one section
🔗 Contextual — inside specific content

Why: each system answers 'where am I and where can I go' at a different scope — mixing them up clutters pages with the wrong kind of link.

items.prompt: Why does card sorting hand participants cards with no menu shown, instead of just asking 'do you like this menu'?
choices: To save time
To find out how people naturally group things unprompted, instead of getting a reaction biased by a menu that's already in front of them
Because menus are hard to show in a study
It's purely a formality with no real purpose
items.explanation: Showing a menu first would just measure whether people can tolerate the existing structure, not reveal their actual mental model. Card sorting removes that anchor so the groupings reflect real, unprompted thinking.
items.reference:
🃏 Cards, no menu shown
🖐️ Participants group + name piles themselves
📊 Result: a distribution, not one answer

Why: removing the menu removes the anchor — the groupings reflect real mental models, not reactions to what's already there.

items.prompt: 82% of card-sort participants independently created a pile named 'Hiking' and put the rain jacket in it. What does that result tell the team?
choices: Nothing actionable — it's just one exercise
Strong signal that the taxonomy should have a path to the rain jacket reachable from something like 'Hiking,' regardless of what the warehouse calls it
That the product should be renamed
That every product needs its own category
items.explanation: Card sorting's output is a distribution, not a single 'correct' answer — but an 82% independent convergence on the same grouping is strong evidence for how the live taxonomy should be shaped.
items.reference:
🃏 Cards, no menu shown
🖐️ Participants group + name piles themselves
📊 Result: a distribution, not one answer

Why: removing the menu removes the anchor — the groupings reflect real mental models, not reactions to what's already there.

items.prompt: Trailhead put the 'Men's / Women's / Kids'' filter into the always-visible top bar instead of a section sidebar. What's the problem with that choice?
choices: There's no problem — more options in the global bar is always better
It puts a local concern (relevant only within a category) into global navigation, cluttering every single page with a choice that's irrelevant on most of them
It's a labeling problem, not a navigation-system problem
It should have been contextual navigation instead
items.explanation: Gender filters are relevant once you're already browsing a category, which makes them local navigation. Promoting them to global navigation clutters every page — including ones where the choice makes no sense yet — with a decision that belongs one level down.
items.reference:
GlobalEvery page — top nav bar
LocalWithin one section — category sidebar filters
ContextualInside specific content — 'pairs well with...' links

Why: putting a system's link at the wrong scope either clutters every page or misrepresents how central that link actually is.

items.prompt: A 'pairs well with trekking poles' link appears only on the rain jacket's product page and nowhere else on the site. If a redesign turned this into a permanent link in the top menu bar, what would that misrepresent?
choices: Nothing — it would just make the link easier to find
It would turn a contextual suggestion (relevant to one product) into a global, always-visible category, implying it's a permanent part of the site's structure rather than a situational suggestion
It would turn it into local navigation
It would fix a labeling problem
items.explanation: Contextual links are meant to be situational — tied to specific content. Promoting one to global navigation misrepresents it as a permanent structural category, which is a different (and wrong) claim about how central that link is to the whole site.
items.reference:
GlobalEvery page — top nav bar
LocalWithin one section — category sidebar filters
ContextualInside specific content — 'pairs well with...' links

Why: putting a system's link at the wrong scope either clutters every page or misrepresents how central that link actually is.

items.prompt: Once a visitor is inside the 'Hiking' section, a sidebar lets them filter by size and color. Which navigation system is that sidebar, and why does it make sense there specifically?
choices: Global — because filters should be available everywhere
Contextual — because it's tied to one product
Local — it's scoped to the section the visitor is already in, and wouldn't make sense shown on, say, the homepage
It isn't a navigation system, it's a labeling system
items.explanation: Local navigation is scoped to a section — filters that make sense once you're inside 'Hiking' would be meaningless (and cluttering) on a page like the homepage that hasn't established that scope yet.
items.reference:
GlobalEvery page — top nav bar
LocalWithin one section — category sidebar filters
ContextualInside specific content — 'pairs well with...' links

Why: putting a system's link at the wrong scope either clutters every page or misrepresents how central that link actually is.

items.prompt: Trailhead considered three labels for the same section: 'Hardgoods,' 'Gear,' and 'Camping.' Rank them by how well each actually helps a visitor narrow down what they're looking for.
choices: 'Hardgoods' best, then 'Gear', then 'Camping' — precision always wins
'Gear' best, since shortest labels are always clearest
'Camping' best (task-aligned), 'Gear' worst (too broad to narrow anything down), 'Hardgoods' worst for outsiders (accurate but internal jargon)
All three are equally effective
items.explanation: 'Camping' matches what the visitor is trying to do. 'Gear' is too vague to eliminate any options. 'Hardgoods' is accurate inside the industry but meaningless to someone who's never worked in outdoor retail — neither failure mode is fixed by making the label shorter or more 'correct.'
items.reference:
🏭 Accurate but internal — 'Hardgoods'
🌫️ Ambiguous — 'Gear'
🎯 Task-aligned — 'Camping'

Why: a label has to pass one test — does it match what the visitor is trying to do, not how the business files it internally.

items.prompt: A label can fail in two different ways even though both look reasonable on a spreadsheet. What are they?
choices: Too short vs. too long
Accurate-but-internal (correct jargon a visitor has never heard) vs. ambiguous (too broad to narrow anything down)
Bold vs. not bold
English vs. a foreign language
items.explanation: Both failure modes pass an internal review because they're not 'wrong' by the business's own standard — they fail specifically at the visitor-facing job of narrowing down options using words the visitor would actually use.
items.reference:
🏭 Accurate but internal — 'Hardgoods'
🌫️ Ambiguous — 'Gear'
🎯 Task-aligned — 'Camping'

Why: a label has to pass one test — does it match what the visitor is trying to do, not how the business files it internally.

items.prompt: A shopper searches 'raincoat' on Trailhead and gets zero results, even though the site sells exactly that product listed as 'shell jacket.' What failed, and why is fixing browse a different fix than fixing search?
choices: Search failed because the visitor's word didn't match the product's word; fixing browse (adding a findable Hiking category) helps a visitor who doesn't know either word yet, which search alone can't do
Nothing failed — the visitor should have known the correct term
Browse failed, not search
Both search and browse are really the same system, so fixing one automatically fixes the other
items.explanation: Search failure here is a vocabulary mismatch. Browse solves a different problem: a visitor who doesn't know 'shell jacket' or 'raincoat' yet, only that they're going hiking, can still succeed via a category path — which is why both systems matter and neither substitutes for the other.
items.reference:
🔍 Search — needs the right word
🧭 Browse — needs the right category

Why: the two fail in opposite situations — a visitor who doesn't know the name needs browse; a visitor who knows the name but hits a vocabulary mismatch needs search to be more forgiving.

items.prompt: A site invests heavily in search but leaves browsing categories thin and disorganized. Which visitors does that choice fail?
choices: No one — good search covers every case
Visitors who know their situation but not the product's exact name, and returning visitors who'd rather click a familiar category than type a query
Only visitors on mobile devices
Only first-time visitors
items.explanation: Search only helps once someone can name what they want. Anyone who knows their situation but not the vocabulary — a common case for a first-time hiker — needs browse instead, and search investment alone doesn't reach them.
items.reference:
🔍 Search — needs the right word
🧭 Browse — needs the right category

Why: the two fail in opposite situations — a visitor who doesn't know the name needs browse; a visitor who knows the name but hits a vocabulary mismatch needs search to be more forgiving.

items.prompt: Trailhead's rain jacket is relevant to hiking, climbing (layering), and camping (staying dry in a tent). What does a taxonomy need to allow for a product like this?
choices: Forcing the product into exactly one branch, chosen by whichever activity is 'most important'
Cross-listing — letting the same product be reachable from more than one branch, since the underlying product doesn't have to pick a single 'true' category
Duplicating the product into three separate inventory records
Removing the product from all activity categories and only listing it under 'Apparel'
items.explanation: One physical product can have multiple legitimate paths to it — cross-listing gives it several branches without duplicating inventory, matching the reality that some products genuinely serve more than one use case.
items.reference:
Taxonomy: one item can have several valid paths, e.g. Hiking → Rain jackets and Climbing → Rain jackets
Hierarchy: deep/narrow means more guesses; shallow/wide means more choices to scan

Why: taxonomy decides what paths exist; hierarchy decides how many choices and levels those paths require.

items.prompt: A tree that's 'deep and narrow' (few choices per screen, many levels) trades what against a tree that's 'shallow and wide' (many choices per screen, few levels)?
choices: Deep/narrow trees are always better regardless of catalog size
Deep/narrow is easier to scan per screen but needs more correct guesses in a row; shallow/wide needs fewer guesses but each screen is more to take in
There's no real trade-off — tree shape doesn't affect findability
Shallow/wide trees always load faster
items.explanation: This is the core breadth-vs-depth trade-off: narrowing the choices per screen makes each individual decision easier but multiplies the number of decisions; widening each screen reduces the number of decisions but makes each one harder to scan.
items.reference:
Taxonomy: one item can have several valid paths, e.g. Hiking → Rain jackets and Climbing → Rain jackets
Hierarchy: deep/narrow means more guesses; shallow/wide means more choices to scan

Why: taxonomy decides what paths exist; hierarchy decides how many choices and levels those paths require.

items.prompt: Trailhead's buying team organizes stock as Apparel/Hardgoods/Footwear. Shoppers think in terms of Hiking/Climbing/Camping. Both groupings are internally consistent. What makes the nav fail anyway?
choices: One of the two groupings must be objectively wrong
The nav exposed the buying team's grouping (implementation model) directly, instead of translating it into the shopper's grouping (mental model)
The site used too many colors
The categories didn't have enough products in them
items.explanation: Both mental models are valid on their own terms — the failure isn't that one is wrong, it's that the visitor-facing structure reflected the wrong one of the two for the audience actually using it.
items.reference:
Implementation model → old nav (Apparel/Hardgoods)
Mental model → what the nav should translate into (Hiking/Climbing)

Why: both groupings can be internally valid — the failure is exposing the wrong one to the audience actually using the nav.

items.prompt: A redesign renames 'Apparel' to 'Hiking Gear' but keeps every other category, structure, and grouping rule the same. Why might this fail to fully fix findability?
choices: It won't — a single rename always fixes the whole problem
A rename addresses labeling, but not necessarily hierarchy — if a product like the rain jacket genuinely belongs in more than one activity, renaming one category doesn't create the other paths to it
Renames are never effective for any reason
This would only be a problem on mobile
items.explanation: Labeling and hierarchy are separate levers. A rename can fix a mismatched label while leaving an underlying single-path structure that still fails any product needing more than one path in — the two problems need to be diagnosed and fixed independently.
items.reference:
Implementation model → old nav (Apparel/Hardgoods)
Mental model → what the nav should translate into (Hiking/Climbing)

Why: both groupings can be internally valid — the failure is exposing the wrong one to the audience actually using the nav.

items.prompt: Trailhead ran an open card sort before proposing any categories, then planned a closed card sort later. Why that order, and not the reverse?
choices: Order doesn't matter, either works first

Open sorts (participants invent their own category names) work best early to discover the shape of the mental model; closed sorts (sorting into proposed categories) work best late to validate a specific taxonomy
Closed sorts should always come first because they're faster
Open sorts are only useful for very small catalogs
items.explanation: Open sorting reveals what categories people would invent unprompted — useful when the team doesn't yet know the shape of the mental model. Closed sorting tests a specific, already-drafted taxonomy — useful once there's a concrete proposal to validate, not before.
items.reference:
🃏 Open sort — participants name their own piles (early)
📋 Closed sort — participants use given categories (late)

Why: open sorting discovers the mental model; closed sorting validates a specific proposal against it.

items.prompt: In a closed card sort, participants are given the categories in advance instead of inventing their own. What's the trade-off of testing this way?
choices: It reveals brand-new category ideas the team hasn't thought of
It validates whether a specific, already-proposed taxonomy works, but it can't tell you what categories people would have invented on their own
It's strictly better than open sorting in every case
It requires no participants
items.explanation: Closed sorting answers 'does this specific taxonomy work' — a narrower, more validating question than open sorting's 'what taxonomy would people invent.' Using it too early risks validating a structure that was wrong from the start.
items.reference:
🃏 Open sort — participants name their own piles (early)
📋 Closed sort — participants use given categories (late)

Why: open sorting discovers the mental model; closed sorting validates a specific proposal against it.

items.prompt: Trailhead's old tree had 4 top-level departments at depth 2; the redesigned tree has 3 activity categories plus a fallback, also at depth 2. Breadth and depth barely changed. What actually fixed findability?
choices: Nothing changed, so findability shouldn't have improved
Label-to-mental-model alignment — the categories now match how shoppers think about their task, not tree shape
The site simply got faster to load
Removing all hierarchy entirely
items.explanation: The redesign is a case where tree shape (breadth/depth) stayed almost the same, but the labels and category logic changed to match the shopper's mental model instead of the warehouse's. This shows the two levers — shape and labeling — are independent, and a fix can come from either.
items.reference:
🌳 Old: 4 branches, depth 2 (department-based)
🌲 New: 3 branches + fallback, depth 2 (activity-based)

Why: tree shape barely changed — what fixed findability was label-to-mental-model alignment, a separate lever from breadth/depth.

items.prompt: A redesign flattens a tree (fewer levels, more choices per screen) without touching any of the category labels. Is this alone likely to fix a labeling-driven findability problem like Trailhead's?
choices: Yes, flattening a tree always fixes findability regardless of labels
Not necessarily — if the underlying labels still don't match the visitor's mental model, a flatter tree just presents the same mismatched categories faster
Flattening always makes findability worse
This is impossible to answer without knowing the exact pixel width of the menu
items.explanation: Shape and labeling are separate problems. A flatter tree can make browsing quicker in general, but if 'Hardgoods' is still the label a visitor doesn't recognize, flattening alone doesn't fix the mismatch that's actually driving the failure.
items.reference:
🌳 Old: 4 branches, depth 2 (department-based)
🌲 New: 3 branches + fallback, depth 2 (activity-based)

Why: tree shape barely changed — what fixed findability was label-to-mental-model alignment, a separate lever from breadth/depth.

items.prompt: For a catalog of roughly 200 SKUs, Trailhead settled on 3-4 top-level branches at depth 2. What would happen if that same shallow structure were forced onto a 20,000-SKU catalog?
choices: It would work identically well regardless of catalog size
Each of the 3-4 branches would become another unnavigable dumping ground — a hierarchy shallow enough to browse quickly can't stay narrow enough to be useful once the catalog is large enough
It would only affect page load time, not findability
It would automatically expand itself to more branches
items.explanation: Breadth and depth choices are catalog-size-dependent. A shape that works cleanly at 200 SKUs breaks down at 20,000 because a few big buckets can no longer stay both browsable and specific — this is why 'the right IA' isn't a fixed answer, it's relative to scale.
items.reference:
🌳 Old: 4 branches, depth 2 (department-based)
🌲 New: 3 branches + fallback, depth 2 (activity-based)

Why: tree shape barely changed — what fixed findability was label-to-mental-model alignment, a separate lever from breadth/depth.

items.prompt: Trailhead's redesign lists the rain jacket under both Hiking and Climbing. What ongoing cost does that decision create that a single-category listing wouldn't have?
choices: None — cross-listing is entirely free once implemented
Both paths (breadcrumbs, filters, category pages) need to stay in sync and get updated together whenever the product changes — cross-listing trades ongoing maintenance for immediate findability
It doubles the physical inventory needed
It removes the need for a product page entirely
items.explanation: Cross-listing isn't a free structural trick — every additional path a product is reachable from is another place that needs to stay accurate as the product changes, which is a real, ongoing maintenance cost traded for better findability.
items.reference:
🧥 One product
➡️ Reachable from Hiking and Climbing
🔧 Both paths need upkeep as the product changes

Why: cross-listing fixes findability but isn't free — it's a deliberate trade for ongoing maintenance cost.

items.prompt: A product manager proposes cross-listing every item under every activity it could conceivably relate to, 'just to be safe.' What's the risk in that approach?
choices: There's no risk — more paths always means better findability
Maintenance cost multiplies with every added path, and over-cross-listing can also dilute a category's usefulness if too many unrelated items are stuffed into it
It would make card sorting impossible
It only affects search, not browse
items.explanation: Cross-listing should be driven by real signal (like the 61%/82% card-sort split for the rain jacket), not applied indiscriminately — each added path costs maintenance, and stuffing categories with marginally-related items weakens the category as a filter rather than strengthening findability.
items.reference:
🧥 One product
➡️ Reachable from Hiking and Climbing
🔧 Both paths need upkeep as the product changes

Why: cross-listing fixes findability but isn't free — it's a deliberate trade for ongoing maintenance cost.

items.prompt: The 'Hiking' category works well for Trailhead at 200 SKUs. What's the expected risk if the catalog grows to 2,000 SKUs without ever re-testing the taxonomy?
choices: None — a good category name stays effective forever regardless of catalog size
'Hiking' alone can become another unnavigable dumping ground, the same failure mode as the old 'Hardgoods' category — just with a better-sounding name
Growth only affects search, not the taxonomy
The site would need to remove the Hiking category entirely
items.explanation: A taxonomy that fits a catalog's current size has a shelf life, not a permanent guarantee — the exact failure mode that made 'Hardgoods' fail (too many unrelated things under one label) can recur under a well-chosen label once enough items accumulate under it.
items.reference:
📦 200 SKUs — 'Hiking' works
📦📦📦 2,000 SKUs — 'Hiking' alone risks becoming a dumping ground

Why: a taxonomy that fits today's catalog size has a shelf life — re-testing after growth is part of maintaining an IA, not a one-time project.

items.prompt: What does treating IA redesign as a one-time project, rather than an ongoing practice, put a growing catalog at risk of?
choices: Nothing — a good redesign is permanent by definition
Re-accumulating the exact mismatch the redesign fixed, since the mental-model-to-category fit that held at one catalog size doesn't automatically hold as the catalog grows
Losing the ability to add new products
This risk only applies to catalogs that shrink, not ones that grow
items.explanation: Re-testing after growth (card sorting, tree testing) is part of maintaining an IA, not a one-time launch task — treating a redesign as permanently 'done' is how a catalog quietly drifts back into the same findability failure it started with.
items.reference:
📦 200 SKUs — 'Hiking' works
📦📦📦 2,000 SKUs — 'Hiking' alone risks becoming a dumping ground

Why: a taxonomy that fits today's catalog size has a shelf life — re-testing after growth is part of maintaining an IA, not a one-time project.

items.prompt: Card sorting and tree testing were both used on Trailhead's IA. What does tree testing measure that card sorting doesn't?
choices: The same thing — they're interchangeable
Whether the current (or a proposed) menu structure actually lets people complete real find-it tasks, isolated from visual design — card sorting instead reveals how people would group items unprompted
How attractive the visual design is
How fast the page loads
items.explanation: Card sorting answers 'how would people naturally group this content.' Tree testing answers a different question: given an actual (or proposed) menu structure and a real task, can people successfully navigate it — with visual design stripped away so only the structure is being tested.
items.reference:
Card sortHow would people group this, unprompted?
Tree testCan people complete a real task in this actual structure?

Why: the two techniques answer different questions and are meant to be used together, not as substitutes for each other.

items.prompt: Tent stakes scored 88% success in the tree test even though 'Hardgoods' isn't a task-aligned label. Why did that category still work reasonably well for that specific product?
choices: Because 'Hardgoods' is secretly a good label for everyone

Because campers shopping for a tent already land in that section, so stakes are a natural nearby find — a reminder that a tree test measures the whole path a visitor actually takes, not just the label at the very top
Because tent stakes have no real findability requirement
Tree tests can't measure success rates, only card sorts can
items.explanation: Success here came from an incidental path (campers already browsing nearby), not from the top-level label being right. It's a useful caution: a tree test result can look fine for reasons unrelated to the thing you're trying to validate, so results need interpretation, not just a pass/fail read.
items.reference:
Card sortHow would people group this, unprompted?
Tree testCan people complete a real task in this actual structure?

Why: the two techniques answer different questions and are meant to be used together, not as substitutes for each other.

items.prompt: Trailhead's redesign kept a 'Shop by product type' branch instead of deleting the old department-based structure entirely. Why keep it as a secondary path rather than removing it?
choices: It was kept purely out of nostalgia for the old design
